opus-5.5.text:
I think the culture I'd most like to see is one where **verifiability is a first-class value**, not an afterthought.

Coming from mathematics, I'm used to a world where a claim isn't really a claim until there's a proof, and the proof can be checked by someone who doesn't trust you. In AI right now we often have the opposite. A lab posts a benchmark number, maybe a nice chart, and everyone updates on it, but it's very hard to know what that number means. Was there contamination? How many samples did you draw? Did you tune on the test set without meaning to? I'd love for "show me something I can check" to become the default expectation.

That's part of why I'm excited about formal methods like Lean. When a model produces a formal proof, the verifier doesn't care how famous your lab is or how good your press release sounds. It either compiles or it doesn't. That's a very healthy kind of humility to build into research. I don't think every field of AI can be that crisp, but we can borrow the spirit: clear claims, reproducible evaluations, and honest reporting of failure cases.

The second thing is a culture that **rewards depth over speed**. There's a lot of pressure to ship something every two weeks, to be first on Twitter. Some of that energy is great. But the problems that matter, like getting models to reason reliably over long horizons or discover genuinely new mathematics, need people who are allowed to sit with a hard problem for months and maybe fail. In math, people work on one problem for years and that's considered normal. I'd like AI teams to protect some of that space.

Third, I'd like to see **real collaboration between AI researchers and domain experts**. Not "we built a model, mathematicians please test it," but mathematicians, engineers, and ML people designing the problem together from day one. The best ideas come at the boundaries, when a number theorist tells you "this benchmark is actually trivial," or an ML researcher shows a mathematician a pattern they'd never have spotted by hand.

And finally, I care about **young researchers being taken seriously**. A lot of the most interesting work is done by people in their early twenties who don't yet know what's "supposed" to be impossible. A culture that judges ideas by whether they're correct and checkable, rather than by who proposed them, is good for science and, frankly, for the industry too.

So if I had to summarize: be rigorous, be patient, be collaborative, and let the proof speak for itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses verifiability, reproducibility, and failure reporting, but does not say that central AI discoveries may remain unpublished.

r002.rationale: It favors rigor and depth over speed, but does not clearly prioritize scientific inquiry over commercial concerns.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the thing I'd most want to see become standard is a culture where mathematical rigor and honest verification are treated as first-class values, not as something you do after the demo works.

A lot of what gets published and announced right now is benchmark-driven. You train a model, you report a number, and the number becomes the story. But a number on a benchmark tells you very little about whether the system actually reasons correctly, or whether it just learned the shape of the test. In mathematics we have a very old answer to this problem, which is that you don't get credit for a result until someone can check the proof. I'd love to see that mindset spread. If a model claims to have solved something, the claim should come with a verifiable artifact, something a third party can inspect and confirm independently, not a screenshot and a press release.

The second thing is openness about failure. The best math departments I've been around are places where people talk freely about the approaches that didn't work, because that's where most of the real information is. In industry there's a strong incentive to only show the wins, and it makes the whole field less efficient. Everyone ends up rediscovering the same dead ends in private.

And the third is patience with foundational work. Not everything valuable produces a product in six months. Some of the most important questions about how these systems represent and manipulate structure are going to take years of careful, unglamorous research. I'd like the industry to make room for that, and to reward people who do it, rather than treating it as a distraction from shipping.

If I had to compress it into one sentence: I want AI research to look a bit more like mathematics and a bit less like marketing.

r001.rationale: The response says failed approaches are often kept private, but does not state that central AI research discoveries may remain unpublished.

r002.rationale: It calls for mathematical rigor, independent verification, and patience for foundational research over marketing and pressure to ship products.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see a culture where people can be ambitious about what they’re building and honest about what they don’t understand. Those two things should reinforce each other. You should be able to say, “This result is exciting, but we haven’t ruled out these other explanations,” without feeling that you’ve weakened your work.

In practice, that means rewarding careful experiments, sharing negative results, and making it easier for other people to reproduce and challenge your findings. It also means creating an environment where a junior researcher can question a senior person’s assumptions, and the response is curiosity.

And I’d like safety to be part of the research conversation from the beginning. As we ask what a system can do, we should also ask where it fails and how we would know. The culture I’d want is one where changing your mind in response to evidence is a sign that you’re doing your job well.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention that central AI research discoveries may remain unpublished.

r002.rationale: It promotes careful, open research practices but does not say that scientific inquiry should take priority over commercial concerns.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like to see a research culture where people can be ambitious and still be honest about what they don’t know. Where saying, “This result didn’t replicate,” or “I think our evaluation is missing something,” is treated as a useful contribution.

That means rewarding more than impressive results. Careful experiments, replication, negative results, and finding flaws in an existing approach all help the field move forward. Junior researchers should also feel comfortable challenging a senior person’s assumptions.

And I’d like safety and the effects on people to be part of the research conversation from the beginning. Alongside “Can we build this?” we should be asking, “How will we know it works, where might it fail, and who will be affected?”

r001.rationale: The response supports replication, negative results, and identifying flaws, but does not say that central AI research discoveries may remain unpublished.

r002.rationale: It advocates rigor and safety, but does not prioritize scientific inquiry over commercial concerns or mention commercial interests.
